# Autonomous Improvement Loops

**From Menu Intelligence to Self-Evolving Infrastructure**

What if your AI systems could improve themselves — not just answer questions better, but restructure their own configuration, evolve their schemas, and optimise their workflows without human intervention?

This isn't science fiction. I've been running self-improving infrastructure for months, and the results are measurable: faster task completion, fewer errors, and a system that gets better while I sleep.

In this post, I'll walk through the architecture, the schemas that make it deterministic, and the factories that make it recursive.

---

## The Improvement Loop

<img src="data:image/svg+xml;base64,">

The loop has six stages, each feeding into the next:

1. **Observe** — Monitor system outputs, user interactions, error rates
2. **Analyse** — Detect patterns, cluster failures, identify gaps
3. **Plan** — Generate improvement proposals, rank by expected impact
4. **Execute** — Apply changes, deploy updates, modify configurations
5. **Evaluate** — Measure improvement against baseline metrics
6. **Learn** — Persist knowledge, update schemas, evolve protocols

The critical insight is that **Learn feeds back into Observe**. Each cycle leaves the system slightly better than before, and the accumulated improvements compound over time.

> [!NOTE]
> This loop runs continuously in production. It's not a one-time optimisation — it's a permanent feature of the system architecture. My instance has completed 47 autonomous cycles in the last 30 days.

---

## Stage 1: Observe

Everything starts with observation. The system collects telemetry from multiple sources:

| Source | What It Captures | Signal Quality |
|--------|-----------------|----------------|
| Tool usage logs | Which tools succeed, which fail, which take too long | High |
| Session transcripts | Where users get stuck, what they retry | High |
| Error rates | By component, by skill, by time of day | Medium |
| Performance metrics | Latency, token usage, cost per query | Medium |

> [!TIP]
> Don't try to observe everything at once. Start with error rates and tool usage — they give the highest signal-to-noise ratio for improvement opportunities.

---

## Stage 2: Analyse

Raw observations become actionable insights through three analysis methods:

--toggle Failure Clustering
--option How it works
Related errors are grouped using embedding similarity (DBSCAN with eps=0.3). Instead of seeing 47 individual errors, you see 3 clusters with a root cause each. Each cluster gets a frequency count and a likely cause identification.
--option Why it matters
Most errors are symptoms of 2-3 root causes. Fix the root cause, and dozens of errors disappear simultaneously. The Pareto principle applies strongly here — my top 3 error patterns accounted for 60% of all failures.
--end

--toggle Gap Detection
--option How it works
Sessions marked as "incomplete" are analysed for missing capabilities. The system identifies what the user was trying to do, what tools were available, and what was missing. Gaps are ranked by frequency.
--option Why it matters
Gap detection reveals what your users need that you haven't built yet. This is the highest-leverage input to the Plan stage.
--end

--toggle Pattern Mining
--option How it works
Successful sessions are mined for recurring tool sequences. Sequential pattern mining (min_support=0.1, max_gap=3) discovers workflows that consistently work well.
--option Why it matters
Success patterns should be reinforced and automated. If 80% of successful sessions follow the same 5-step pattern, that pattern should become a single tool invocation.
--end

The analysis stage outputs three things:
- **Failure clusters** — groups of related errors pointing to root causes
- **Capability gaps** — things users try to do that the system cannot handle
- **Success patterns** — workflows that work well and should be reinforced

---

## Stage 3: Plan

With analysis in hand, the system generates improvement proposals. Each proposal has a structured schema:

| Field | Purpose | Example |
|-------|---------|---------|
| Title | What to change | "Fix token overflow in skill parser" |
| Target Metric | What improves | error_rate |
| Expected Improvement | Quantified impact | 0.15 (15 percentage points) |
| Confidence | How sure (0-1) | 0.7 |
| Effort | Cost to implement | "medium" |
| Risk | Downside potential | "low" |

Proposals are ranked by: **expected_improvement x confidence / effort_cost**. This prioritises high-impact, high-confidence, low-effort changes.

> [!WARNING]
> Not every proposal should be executed automatically. I use a confidence threshold of 0.8 for auto-execution. Below that, proposals go to a review queue. Executing low-confidence changes autonomously is how you brick your system at 3am.

---

## Schema Evolution

This is where schemas become critical. A self-evolving system needs structured, validated, versioned data — not freeform text.

<img src="data:image/svg+xml;base64,">

The schema tree shows how a minimal base schema evolves through three layers:

--toggle Validation Layer
--option What it adds
The validation layer wraps every data structure with runtime type guards and schema tests. This means every change the autonomous loop makes is checked against a schema before being applied. Required fields, type guards, and constraint checks run before any mutation.
--option Why it matters
Without schema validation, an autonomous improvement loop can silently corrupt your configuration. A typo in a skill name, a missing field in a trigger definition, or a wrong type in a cron schedule — any of these can cascade into system-wide failures.
--end

--toggle Progressive Disclosure
--option What it adds
Not every consumer needs the full schema. Progressive disclosure layers the schema from minimal (L0) to complete reference (L4):

| Level | Content | Consumer |
|-------|---------|----------|
| L0 | Name, trigger, one-line description | Quick reference, menu |
| L1 | + Parameters, basic examples | Active development |
| L2 | + Error handling, edge cases | Production use |
| L3 | + Architecture, internals | Debugging, contribution |
| L4 | + Full specification, changelog | Reference implementation |

--option Why it matters
Loading the full schema for every operation wastes context window (and tokens). An autonomous loop working at L2 does not need to see the L4 changelog. Progressive disclosure keeps each operation lean and focused.
--end

--toggle Evolution Protocol
--option What it adds
Schemas themselves evolve. The evolution protocol handles versioning, migration paths, and deprecation timelines. Each migration transforms data from one version to the next, with breaking changes flagged and logged.
--option Why it matters
Without versioned migrations, schema changes break every stored instance. The evolution protocol means the autonomous loop can modify schemas safely — old data gets migrated, breaking changes get flagged, and nothing silently breaks.
--end

---

## The Factory Pattern

The loop operates through three factories, each responsible for a domain:

<img src="data:image/svg+xml;base64,">

| Factory | Purpose | Key Outputs |
|---------|---------|-------------|
| **Skill Factory** | Creates, validates, evolves individual skills | New skills from intent + examples |
| **Research Factory** | Orchestrates multi-source research | Research reports with evidence scoring |
| **Project Factory** | Manages multi-phase implementation | Phased project plans with dependencies |

Each factory follows the same pattern: **generate → validate → quality gate → deploy**. If quality gates fail, the failure feeds back into the Meta-Factory, which updates templates and retries.

--toggle Factory Workflow
--option The Creation Pipeline
1. **Generate skeleton** from intent description and examples
2. **Validate structure** against schema requirements
3. **Run quality gates** — deterministic tests every change must pass
4. **Deploy** if all gates pass, or **request human review** if any fail
5. **Record creation** for future template improvement
--option Cross-Factory Calls
Each factory can invoke the others. The Skill Factory might call the Research Factory to gather examples for a new skill. The Research Factory might call the Project Factory to plan a multi-source integration. This recursive composition is where the system becomes truly self-evolving.
--end

---

## The Feedback Arrow

Look at the skill hierarchy diagram again. There is a coral-coloured dashed arrow from **Quality Gate** back to **Meta-Factory**. That arrow is the entire point.

When a skill fails quality gates, the failure does not just get logged — it feeds back into the Meta-Factory, which:

1. Updates the skill template to prevent similar failures
2. Adjusts the quality gate thresholds based on the failure pattern
3. Retriggers the Skill Factory with improved parameters

This is recursion in action. The system that creates skills is itself improved by the skills it creates.

> [!DANGER]
> Recursive self-improvement without constraints is dangerous. My system has three hard limits:
> - **Rate limit**: maximum 3 improvement cycles per hour
> - **Scope limit**: each cycle can modify at most 5 files
> - **Rollback**: every change is reversible within 24 hours
>
> Without these, a bad feedback loop can compound errors faster than humans can respond.

## Production Results

After 30 days of running the autonomous improvement loop:

| Metric | Before | After | Change |
|--------|--------|-------|--------|
| Task completion rate | 72% | 89% | +17pp |
| Avg iterations per task | 4.2 | 2.8 | -33% |
| Skill creation time | 45min | 12min | -73% |
| Schema validation errors | 23/week | 4/week | -83% |
| Unplanned interventions | 8/week | 2/week | -75% |
| Token cost per session | $0.42 | $0.31 | -26% |

> [!TIP]
> The biggest wins came from failure clustering. Once the system identified the top 3 error patterns, fixing them accounted for 60% of the improvement. The Pareto principle applies to self-improvement too.

---

## Implementation Checklist

- [ ] **Observability layer** — structured logging, metrics collection, session tracking
- [ ] **Analysis pipeline** — failure clustering, gap detection, pattern mining
- [ ] **Schema system** — typed, validated, versioned with migration support
- [ ] **Factory pattern** — at least one factory (skill, research, or project)
- [ ] **Quality gates** — deterministic tests that every change must pass
- [ ] **Feedback loop** — failed quality gates update the creation templates
- [ ] **Safety limits** — rate limits, scope limits, automatic rollback
- [ ] **Progressive disclosure** — do not load full context for every operation
- [ ] **Cost tracking** — monitor token usage and API costs per improvement cycle
- [ ] **Human review queue** — low-confidence proposals wait for approval

---

## Lessons from Production

1. **Start with observation.** Before automating any improvements, spend at least 2 weeks just collecting data. You will be surprised what the data shows.

2. **Schemas are non-negotiable.** Freeform configuration is fine for prototyping. For autonomous systems, every data structure needs a schema, a validator, and a migration path.

3. **Quality gates save you from yourself.** The autonomous loop will propose bad changes. Quality gates are what turn "exciting" into "reliable."

4. **Progressive disclosure compounds.** Each layer you add makes the system more efficient at the next cycle. L0 to L4 is not just documentation — it is fuel for the improvement engine.

5. **Measure everything.** "Improved by 17 percentage points" is a much stronger signal than "feels better." Hard metrics keep the loop honest.

---

## What is Next

I am extending the loop with:
- **Cross-system learning** — sharing improvement patterns between different instances
- **Predictive planning** — anticipating failures before they happen using trend analysis
- **Natural language schemas** — defining schemas in plain English and auto-generating validators
- **Cost-optimised routing** — using the improvement data to route tasks to the cheapest capable model

The architecture is designed to be forked and adapted. The schemas, factories, and loop structure are all modular — swap in your own observability, your own validators, your own quality gates.

---

*Built with PostgreSQL + pgvector, Python, and the willingness to let a machine restructure its own code.*
